summary.text: The Arctic ice pack is the sea ice that covers the Arctic Ocean and the waters around it.
It melts through spring and summer to a low around mid-September, then grows again in autumn and winter, with summer cover about half of winter cover.
Beneath that yearly rhythm the ice has been declining for decades, with the minimum extent dropping by over a million square kilometres in 2007 and hitting a new record low in 2012.

facts.value: Summer cover about 50% of winter cover

items.prompt: Fresh snow falls on a stretch of bare Arctic sea ice. What happens to the share of sunlight that surface reflects?

options.label: It drops, since snow soaks up light
It stays exactly the same as before
It rises, since snowy ice is brighter
It falls to match the open sea

items.explain: Bare sea ice reflects about 60% of incoming sunlight, and snow-covered ice about 80%.

items.prompt: As Arctic seawater freezes in winter, what happens to the water left just beneath the new ice?

options.label: It gets saltier and denser, and sinks
It gets fresher and lighter, and rises
It warms up and melts the ice above
It stays exactly as it was before

items.explain: Freezing leaves most of the salt behind, so the remaining surface water becomes dense and sinks, forming water masses such as North Atlantic Deep Water.

items.prompt: In midwinter the Arctic air is far colder than the sea beneath it. What does a cover of sea ice do in that situation?

options.label: It speeds up heat flowing from sea to air
It cools the ocean below by trapping cold
It lets the cold air chill the deep ocean
It cuts the heat the ocean loses to the air

items.explain: Sea ice insulates the relatively warm ocean from the much colder air, reducing heat loss from the ocean.

items.prompt: Two Septembers show the same Arctic ice area, but in the second year the ice is much thinner. What would a measure of ice volume show?

options.label: The same amount of ice in both years
Less ice in the second year
More ice in the second year
Nothing, since volume ignores thickness

items.explain: Ice volume depends on thickness as well as area, so thinner ice over the same area means less ice overall.

items.prompt: More and more Arctic ice is now thin first-year ice. What tends to happen when a major storm passes over it?

options.label: The storm piles it into thick, stable ridges
The ice is unaffected by passing storms
The storm freezes it into thicker sheets
The ice cracks into extensive fractures

items.explain: Thinner first-year ice is less stable, and turbulence from major storms causes extensive fractures in it.

items.prompt: At its yearly low in late summer, how much Arctic ice cover is left compared with the winter peak?

options.label: Under 5% of it
About half of it
About 90% of it
The same as winter

items.explain: Summer ice cover in the Arctic is about 50% of winter cover.
